title: Checkpoint: Daily Life
objective: After this level you can describe home, food, work and fun in ancient Egypt.
summary: Kings carved their deeds in stone; ordinary Egyptians left clues. Teeth, fingerprints, lost towns and the everyday writing of Deir el-Medina show how people lived.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale: how do we know what ordinary Egyptians ate, did and loved?
cards.body: Kings carved their deeds in stone. Everyone else left clues: teeth, fingerprints, scraps of pottery. Time to play detective with this chapter’s evidence.

cards.headline: Clues nobody meant to leave
cards.body: Some evidence was never meant as a record. Worn-down teeth show that Egyptian bread was gritty with sand. Fingerprints in clay moulds show children as young as ten at work in workshops. Even what’s missing is a clue: ordinary homes mostly vanished because towns stood in the flooded valley, while temples and tombs stood where the flood couldn’t reach.

cards.headline: Clues people wrote down
cards.body: Then there’s writing, and the tomb builders’ village is our richest source: its papyri and ostraca show details of daily life rarely seen anywhere else in Egypt. A limestone flake lists a worker absent for brewing beer. A papyrus records hungry workmen striking over late rations. Naunakhte’s will cuts out children who didn’t care for her. Outsiders add their own notes, like Herodotus on families shaving their eyebrows for a dead cat. Put together, you meet a people who worked hard, ate bread, drank beer and loved their cats.

cards.headline: Chapter 6 complete
learned: How historians rebuild ordinary lives from worn teeth, fingerprints and everyday notes.
Why bread and beer were the staples, and how food rations served as wages.
How Egyptian women had nearly equal rights in law but not in daily life.
Why so few homes survive, when houses were mud brick and stone was saved for temples and tombs.

questions.prompt: Daily life recap: why have so few ordinary Egyptian homes survived?

options.label: Pharaohs ordered all houses torn down
options.rationale: The problem was where towns stood.

options.label: Towns stood in the flooded valley, and houses were mud brick
Egyptians lived only in tents
Earthquakes destroyed every town
options.rationale: The flood and the soft mud brick were the problem.

questions.explanation: Mud-brick towns in the cultivated, flooded valley were lost, while stone temples and tombs above the flood survived.

questions.prompt: Daily life recap: which Egyptian game was played on 30 squares in three rows of ten?

options.label: Mehen
options.rationale: Mehen used a spiral, coiled-snake board.

options.label: Senet
Chess
options.rationale: Chess came much later, from elsewhere.

options.label: Checkers

questions.explanation: Senet used 30 squares in three rows of ten, with casting sticks for dice.

questions.prompt: Daily life recap: what makes the Turin papyrus about Deir el-Medina’s workmen so historic?

options.label: It is the oldest papyrus ever found
options.rationale: Its fame comes from what it records.

options.label: It records the first known strike, over late rations
It lists the pharaoh’s favorite foods
It is Naunakhte’s will
options.rationale: Her will is a different document.

questions.explanation: The scribe Amunnakht recorded hungry workmen stopping work over late grain rations: the first recorded strike.

questions.prompt: Daily life recap: what does Naunakhte’s will show about Egyptian women?

options.label: They could not own property
options.rationale: Her will divided her own property.

options.label: They needed a husband’s permission to make a will
options.rationale: Her property was separate from her husband’s.

options.label: A woman could decide who inherited her property
Only queens had legal rights
options.rationale: Naunakhte was a villager, not a queen.

questions.explanation: Naunakhte chose which children inherited from her and left out those who hadn’t cared for her.

questions.prompt: Daily life recap: how did Egypt’s cats connect to the crops of Level 4?

options.label: Cats pulled the plows
Cats guarded the grain from rodents
Cats trod seed into the soil
Cats were fed only on barley
options.rationale: Their job was catching the rodents that ate it.

questions.explanation: Cats hunted the rodents that threatened Egypt’s wheat and barley.
